Many people have suggested over the decades that the various job descriptions are so different that perhaps they should each have different names. I had always believed that it would be very hard to get an entire industry to change something as entrenched as one of the major job titles, and that it likely wouldn’t be worth the effort. I’m no longer so sure about that. Today we have the situation where some major industry leaders proclaim the product role is dead, and others proclaim that it’s the single most important role going forward.  Each very likely assumes the other is clueless. What most don’t realize, including many of the industry leaders, is that the operating model a company uses to create products is what drives the roles and responsibilities of the members of the teams, and we have long had two very different operating models in play. This has caused some relatively minor confusions when it comes to the role of product designers and engineers, but it has caused very significant confusion when it comes to the role of the product manager. Beyond the long-standing confusion, AI is now shining a very bright light on this topic, and finally forcing the industry to take a hard look at this role.   That hard look is the subject of this article. The Three Different Definitions of the Product Role The most fundamental reason there are different definitions of the product role is because there are different operating models for creating products , and the operating model drives what roles and skills are needed. When using the project model , there are two different product roles, although it is not uncommon for companies to have both: the feature team product manager and the agile product owner . When using the product model , we have the empowered team product manager . Each of these three roles has very different responsibilities and requires very different skills, yet so many in the product community seem to behave as if there is only one (usually the one they are doing). Note that I am not including product leaders here; I’m just speaking to the people responsible for product creation . In addition to trying to clearly state the differences between the three roles, I will share my view on AI’s impact to each: which versions of the role we can expect will lose their relevance and are likely to disappear, and which will become increasingly important and prominent. The Project Model  In a company using the project model, the product roadmap contains prioritized features and projects, which are each a hoped-for solution to some usually unstated problem.  Projects and features are funded and staffed, and success is defined by shipping this solution. The job of the feature team is to design, build, QA test, and deploy that particular hoped-for solution.  There is very little, if any, product discovery because the solution has already been prescribed.  It’s all about turning this feature or project into a solution that can be shipped (aka build to earn ).  The Feature Team Product Manager role:   The job of the feature team product manager in this model is to marshal and coordinate the resources required to get this solution designed, built, tested, and shipped.   In this situation, the feature team product manager is essentially playing a project management role to drive the execution .  This often includes helping out wherever needed, which is why these people can end up writing documentation one day, performing QA the next day, and committing simple front-end code changes the next. Today companies are racing to use agentic AI to automate as much of the delivery process as possible, striving to create a software factory where agents handle the work that was previously handled by developers, QA, release managers, and feature team product managers, and engineers oversee and direct the various agents performing these tasks.   It is clear that there is less need for feature team product managers, but it is less clear how many may still be needed to provide some level of oversight beyond what the engineers and their agents can do. The Product Owner role:   For project model companies using Agile (like Scrum or Kanban) or SAFe, this is a role in the delivery process, managing the delivery backlog, and coordinating with the engineers before, during and after sprints. 1 Today, with AI disrupting the delivery process by both automating and accelerating the engineering activities and workflows, and with so much of the sprint process obviated, the product owner role is already being phased out.
